top_choice_rationale: P001 (Helpman and Melitz, B010) rewards one identifiable discovery: firm heterogeneity and selection in trade theory. It explains who exports, why exporters differ systematically, and how liberalisation reallocates activity across firms. These predictions go beyond what representative-firm new trade theory generates, and they have been tested on firm-level data in many countries for over twenty years, so maturity is not in doubt. A two-name credit follows the intellectual structure: Melitz (2003) is the core model, and Helpman, including Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple on exporting versus foreign investment, completes the framework. The main costs are the omitted precursors (Bernard, Jensen, Eaton, Kortum, Hopenhayn) and Redding's later extensions. A narrow citation on selection and reallocation, with the precursors credited in the scientific background, handles these reasonably. The size of the welfare gains depends on distributional assumptions, so the citation should rest on the mechanism and not on a welfare number. I do not treat the eleven-member support as merit, only as evidence that attribution is stable across assessors. Because P001 is the only substantive proposal, I rank no award last, as it is clearly worse than a defensible, mature and well-attributed contribution.
recusal_note: None apparent from profile regarding Helpman or Melitz. Disclosed, not adjudicated: I am a frequent co-author of John Hassler (chair) and have co-authored with Timo Boppart (co-opted member). Both support P001 but are not candidates. My field, heterogeneous-agent macro and growth, is adjacent to the micro-to-macro reallocation questions in B010.
